newsitem.title: japan: OLYMPICS-IOC OFFICIAL CRITICISES "OUTDATED" GENDER TESTS.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-IOC OFFICIAL CRITICISES "OUTDATED" GENDER TESTS.

text.p: Gender testing for female Olympic athletes should be improved or abandoned before the 2000 Sydney Games, an Olympic medical official said on Sunday.

The pre-competition chromosome test which all female athletes have been required to undergo since the 1968 Mexico City Olympics had been outdated by rapid advances in the field of genetics, Arne Ljungqvist of Sweden, a member of the International Olympic Committee (IOC) medical commission, told Reuters.
"I think this is something that will have to be corrected before Sydney," he said.
Medical commission chief Prince Alexandre de Merode defended the tests, saying that the IOC had a responsibility to ensure that no men competed in women's events.

"The international federations have competitions for men and for women and we have to be very sure everybody is competing in their own sector," said de Merode after a meeting of the IOC medical commission in Nagano.
But Ljungqvist said the chromosome test did not fulfill that aim.
"There are men with chromosomes like females and vice versa," he said. "If we screen for sex by using this test, women will be screened out and men will pass."
Gender testers at the Atlanta Olympics recommended last month that the IOC abandon the chromosome test, Ljungqvist said.

About one in 400 females in Atlanta tested male but all were cleared by subsequent physical examinations, he said. If the IOC wanted to continue gender testing, Atlanta medical officials recommended random physical inspections.

The International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) abandoned gender testing in 1992, said Ljungqvist, who also heads its medical commission. The Commonwealth and World University Games followed suit.

Only five of 34 Olympic federations still conducted gender tests at their own world championships, he said. The American Medical Association recommended five years ago that all sports stop gender testing.

The test, in which cells are scraped from the inside of the cheek, was also unnecessary because modern doping controls required athletes to urinate in the presence of a medical official, Ljungqvist said.
Widespread media coverage of international sport had also reduced the chances of men successfully competing as women, he added.

French and Spanish scientists protested about the use of the chromosome test before the 1992 Albertville and Barcelona Olympics, said Ljungqvist. The Albertville team were called on to perform the tests two years later at the Lillehammer Games after Norwegian medical officials refused, he added.
The chromosome test had survived only because female athletes were unaware of its shortcomings, said Ljungqvist.
"The opposition has to come from the affected group," he said.
